prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

compared to a traditional crosswalk. Car drivers have similar perceptions, with 65.3 % rating the 3D crosswalk as safer or much safer for pedestrian crossing in comparison to a traditional crosswalk. It is important to note that the perceived level of safety, does not necessarily correspond to the actual level of safety (Cho et al., 2009), and that road users might compensate for a higher level of perceived safety, by showing riskier behavior (Wilde, 1982). In this study, only the perceptions of road users were investigated, which does not allow a direct transfer to actual behavior. For road users’ perceptions of increased safety of road crossings on the 3D crosswalk in comparison to traditional crosswalks, there are a number of potential reasons. Unrelated to the 3D effect of the crosswalk, road users could perceive the painted area of the 3D crosswalk as larger compared to traditional crosswalks. The drawing pattern used to produce the optical illusion of the 3D crosswalk (Fig. 2) breaks apart the straight lines that make up a traditional crosswalk, which could lead to a perceived increase of the painted area, and thereby the perceived visibility of the 3D crosswalk. Related to this, road users might compare the visibility of the newly painted 3D crosswalk to the average visibility of older traditional crosswalks that they encounter in the road system. As the majority of traditional crosswalks that road users encounter will be considerably older than the 3D crosswalk, their paint will have faded more, potentially decreasing objective as well as perceived visibility of traditional crosswalks in comparison to the new 3D crosswalk. Increased safety perceptions due to a perceived larger painted area and higher color intensity of the 3D crosswalk would be in line with research that shows a relation between the visibility of a crosswalk and pedestrian safety (Feldman, Manzi, & Mitman, 2010; Fitz- patrick, Chrysler, Iragavarapu, & Park, 2011; Guo, & Boyle, 2022; Pulugurtha, Vasudevan, Nambisan, & Dangeti, 2012; Sarwar et al., 219 F.W. Many observers (e.g., Palafox, 2022) have noted how cars have been the priority in road design in the country, and the experience of the walking tour simply illustrates this bias. The sensory evaluation of the walking experiences such as comments on foul smells, trash, and pollution, highlighted the physical challenges faced by participants. Here, the value of the individual participants’ perception of the surrounding world, or sensescapes (Agapito et al., 2013), heightened awareness of the physical conditions, with comments on the “foul smell of the Pasig River”, “areas filled with trash that stink” and the “smog/polluted air is not safe for elderly/pregnant women to walk”, as the well as more general remarks on the heat. A male participant summarized all these as the convergence of 4 Ws – weather, walkways, wheels, and water. For the UP-Walking Tours participants, the experience was a bit different. Participants did not say much about infrastructure issues in the university, although some did mention the need to have “stops with seats” and a “place to leave personal belongings”. Besides the constant refrain on the heat and the acoustic environment, there was not much comment on the physical environment or danger from passing cars. This is perhaps a reflection of how the academic community operates in privileged seclusion and how, in general, the built environment can shape active transport experience (Agyeman and Doran, 2021). 4.2. Paths and paved areas in roadside green spaces shall meet the following requirements: 1. The material and thickness of the paving surface layer shall be coordinated with the road greening style and use function, and integrated with sponge city design. Traffic-function roads The sides of traffic-function roads are mainly non-open interfaces, with relatively few non-traffic activities, and the paved areas mainly serve traffic distribution functions. Paving design shall implement the concepts of safety, health, comfort, and people-oriented design. Figure 1.4-2 Example of paving for traffic-function roads B. Living-service roads The activity groups on living-service roads include residents and workers around the road, as well as people from other areas who come for shopping and strolling. In terms of paving materials, color, texture, and grain, attention shall be paid to people’s perceptions, and localized creative design shall be applied to road entrances to enrich the walking experience. As a city streetscape evaluation expert, please analyze the uploaded streetscape image based on the specified persona perspective and evaluation indicators, and return a JSON result.
 Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)
Current Selection:
All Road Users; All Social Groups
 Indicator Selection
Justice
- Equity
- Fairness
- Accessibility
Safety
Livability
Sustainability
Aesthetics
Comfort
- Thermal Comfort
- Physical Comfort
- Psychological Comfort
Walkability
Bikeability
Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.
 4. Output Format Requirements (Return JSON ONLY, no extra text):

Car drivers have similar perceptions, with 65.3 % rating the 3D crosswalk as safer or much safer for pedestrian crossing in comparison to a traditional crosswalk. It is important to note that the perceived level of safety, does not necessarily correspond to the actual level of safety (Cho et al., 2009), and that road users might compensate for a higher level of perceived safety, by showing riskier behavior (Wilde, 1982). In this study, only the perceptions of road users were investigated, which does not allow a direct transfer to actual behavior. For road users’ perceptions of increased safety of road crossings on the 3D crosswalk in comparison to traditional crosswalks, there are a number of potential reasons. Unrelated to the 3D effect of the crosswalk, road users could perceive the painted area of the 3D crosswalk as larger compared to traditional crosswalks. The drawing pattern used to produce the optical illusion of the 3D crosswalk (Fig. 2) breaks apart the straight lines that make up a traditional crosswalk, which could lead to a perceived increase of the painted area, and thereby the perceived visibility of the 3D crosswalk. Related to this, road users might compare the visibility of the newly painted 3D crosswalk to the average visibility of older traditional crosswalks that they encounter in the road system. As the majority of traditional crosswalks that road users encounter will be considerably older than the 3D crosswalk, their paint will have faded more, potentially decreasing objective as well as perceived visibility of traditional crosswalks in comparison to the new 3D crosswalk. Increased safety perceptions due to a perceived larger painted area and higher color intensity of the 3D crosswalk would be in line with research that shows a relation between the visibility of a crosswalk and pedestrian safety (Feldman, Manzi, & Mitman, 2010; Fitz- patrick, Chrysler, Iragavarapu, & Park, 2011; Guo, & Boyle, 2022; Pulugurtha, Vasudevan, Nambisan, & Dangeti, 2012; Sarwar et al., 219 F.W.
